property_description: The Alewine property is 95.9 acres of pristine mountain lands which adjoins scenic Highway 11 with the Jocassee Gorges Wildlife Management Area. In addition to the high natural resources value of this property, it is a key acquisition from a public access standpoint. The current size of Jocassee Gorge is 33,430 acres, of which a significant portion are inaccessible to the public due to a lack of road access. This piece of property has allowed solid public access to 3000 acres of previously inaccessible lands. The Alewine lands have also provided space for a Department of Natural Resources workshed and storage facility, both of which assist DNR in their management of the park. The land is primarily older aged mixed hardwood forest with extensive river frontage. The acquisition of this land ensures protection of headwater seeps and streams of the Oolenoy River as well as providing excellent habitat for game species, fish and birds, resting and feeding areas for migratory species and critical habitat corridors.
notes: Part of SCDNR's Jocassee Gorges
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The acquisition of the Alexander Tract represents the final link in the joining together of 16,000 acres of park lands located in North and South Carolina. This land was purchased for inclusion in Kings Mountain State Park located in Cherokee County. The Alexander Tract opened up vast amounts of land to the public for hunting, fishing, canoeing, biking, educational opportunities as well as charitable organizations such as the Make-A-Wish Foundation. The South Carolina Department of Parks, Recreation and Tourism contributed funds along with the Conservation Bank to make the addition of the Alexander Tract a possibility.

Fishing Creek provides habitat for the federally endangered Carolina Heelsplitter.

When the typical visitor to Caesar's Head looks down toward Table Rock, they are seeing the Asbury Hills tract. The land is 98% forested and would have been in immediate danger of development if the Conservation Bank had not secured funds.

property_description: Protection of the Asbury Hills Expansion property is significant for providing habitat linkagesAsbury Hills within South Carolina's mountain forests and streams. The property is entirely forested with Southern Blue Ridge forest types of mainly Pine-Oak Heath and Oak-hickory forests. These forests support excellent wildlife habitat for game species such as turkey, deer and black bear. There are rare, non-game species that have been documented on and around the property such as Appalachian cottontail, Woodland jumping mouse, six bat species including Northern Long-eared bat and Rafineque's Big-eared bat, plus neotropical migratory birds such as Swainson's warbler. The property's forested environment filters two streams traversing through the property, which are headwater streams to the S. Saluda River and flow to Lake Saluda, a recreation lake that supplies water to the town of Easley, SC. This property will add and be compatible to the already conserved 1,892 acres held under a conservation easement with TNC. The Camp intends to use the property for passive recreation for their camp and retreat programs. This property was enrolled into the SC DNR Wildlife Management Agreement (WMA) Program, adding to the Asbury Hills property already in WMA.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract makes up roughly one third of the entire Ashley River Plantation District. The area is an ecologically diverse region containing historical landmarks that are constantly threatened by development in the Charleston and Summerville areas.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract represents the first grant in Clarendon County by the Conservation Bank. The tract is a family farm and also acts as a waterfowl hunting property. This is in the area known as the Santee Waterfowl Corridor and is the first project to go up and down the Upper Santee Swamp. This tract will be used for controlled waterfowl hunting while also aiding in water quality for the area.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Bailey Mill is a magnificent piece of relatively undeveloped property in Jasper County. The property is currently used for hunting, timber and agricultural activities. It is prominently visible by the public from Bailey Mill Road, having approximately 1,900 feet of scenic road frontage. Bailey Mill lies within the more than 2 millions acres of the South Lowcountry (SoLo) Focus Area featuring diverse ecosystems and a wealth of wildlife. This property contains a diversity of relatively natural habitats including upland pine forest and forested and un-forested wetlands in various stages of succession, and open fields, all of which can support a variety of floral and faunal species. Baily Mill lies within Calfpen Bay and flows into the Great Swamps. It is within the headwaters of the New River and runs into the Port Royal Sound.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Barker Association tract represents an ongoing effort by the Bank to help preserve lands along the Savannah River. As part of the Savannah River Preserve program, landowners donate the easements at the cost of $208 an acre. This tract of land is within the Savannah River Watershed and is a key acquisition for water quality protection.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Batten-Boggy Tract is located in Hampton County approximately 4 miles west of the Town of Garnett and encompasses 315 acres of heavily forested land dominated by upland pine and bottomland hardwood swamp. A total of 112 acres of wetlands occur on the property including bottomland hardwoods, gum ponds, and pine hardwood flats. Uplands consists of 138 acres of planted loblolly pine, 13 acres of hardwood hammock, 11 acres of open wildlife food plot, and 41 acres of cutover/open lands.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Battery Wilkes Tract houses an important piece of South Carolina history in Charleston County. The property saves a Civil War fortification listed on the National Register of Historic Places and one of only fifty or fewer remaining fortification sites out of the 183 that once existed in Charleston County. It is located on the Savannah Hwy with the hopes of becoming part of the City of Charleston and a public park.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Battle of Handing Rock property, located in Heath Spring, was a portion of the battlefield for the August 6, 1780, Battle of Hanging Rock. This significant Revolutionary War battle was the first in a series of battles as American Patriots attempted to threaten British strongholds in the upcounty of the state.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_name: Battle of Parker's Ferry - Liberty Trail
transfer_to: Colleton Co. or Colleton Co. Historical Society
property_description: In the summer of 1781, British and Loyalist troops were operating in the countryside outside of Charleston, both foraging for provisions and attempting to suppress the Patriot militia. Militia Colonel William Harden commanded a small force south of the Edisto River and asked for assistance in dealing with the British patrols. On August 10, 1781, Major General Nathanael Greene dispatched Brigadier General Francis Marion to assist Harden. Arriving on August 22, Marion learned that a Loyalist force commanded by William "Bloody Bill" Cunningham was at Pon Pon River (present-day Edisto River) to join a much larger force of British regulars, Hessian troops, and other Loyalist militia. Parker's Ferry was a major thoroughfare crossing the river and it was here that Marion planned his ambush. On August 30, Marion placed his troops in the thick woods about forty yards from the causeway leading to Parker's Ferry. Marion sent several dragoons forward to entice the Loyalist troops to follow them into the trap. As shots were fired, British Lt. Colonel Ernst Leopold von Borek ordered Major Thomas Fraser and his dragoons to charge to the scene. Fraser's troops galloped blindly into the "gauntlet" that Marion set for them. British causalities were heavy, while Marion only had one man killed and three wounded. This fight was effective in forcing the British cavalry back to Charleston, never to return to the Jacksonborough region. As a result, the dragoons with von Borek were not available to fight at the Battle of Eutaw Springs just eight days later. Marion pulled back to the Santee and joined Greene for this important battle in which he commanded the militia battle line, the front line to engage the British. This project preserves all of the footprint of the core of the Battle of Parker's Ferry. This battle is the quintessential example of the ambush tactics under by Brigadier General Francis Marion during the war. Preserving this battlefield will be a significant addition to the SC Liberty Trail.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_name: Battle of Port Royal (Harris Pillow) - Liberty Trail
match_notes: Marine Corps Air Station, Beaufort County (estimated)
property_description: In January 1779, British Major William Gardner was ordered to make a naval landing and march infantry companies to occupy Port Royal Island. Learning of the British advance, Patriot General Benjamin Lincoln dispatched Brigadier General William Moultrie to meet this British Threat.  The battle is significant for a number of reasons. If the British were successful in capturing Port Royal, they would have controlled the largest natural deep-water harbor south of New York. Secondly, both Thomas Heyward, Jr. and Edward Rutledge fought in the battle.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Baxley lands represents 979 acres of prime farmland in Marion County. This land has been put into an easement with matching funds from the USDA's Farm and Ranchland Protection Program. Together, these funds will ensure that the farming way of life will continue to exist in the area, despite developmental pressures from nearby Myrtle Beach. Many farms in this area were once Carolina Bays which have long since been drained, resulting in unusual systems of canals and crossdrains. The Conservation Bank was a key partner in helping to maintain this farming community’s way of life.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract has 9.9 miles of frontage on Little River and other tributaries. It is largely a timber tract and managed for traditional use. This tract and the future adjoining tract of 16,000 acres are the SCNDR number one priorities statewide, and they will be receiving most of the available Heritage Trust funds for an extended period of time. This tract adjoins a state park and has a historic house on site built in 1865. This tract will become part of the Last Great Places initiative. The Bank does not currently have any grants in Newberry County and very few in Laurens County.
notes: Part of SCDNR's Belfast Wildlife Management Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Bell Buoy Tract is a spectacular piece of land on Edisto Beach. It is deepwater property along Big Bay Creek, in the heart of the ACE Basin. Protecting land along this creek is in accordance with the ACE Basin Land Protection and Enhancement Plan. Aside from its significance to the ACE Basin this piece of property is of the utmost importance to the Town of Edisto Beach. This property is the last vestige of a formerly strong local shrimping industry and protection ensures an ample sample of fresh seafood. Rather then being turned into private expensive condos, or a dock for a casino boat, the Bell Buoy land provides public access to deepwater along the creek. The owners of the property were willing to donate $ 1.5 million of the purchase price to the town to express their desire that this land remain open to the public. The South Carolina Conservation Bank's funding was of critical assistance to the Town of Edisto Beach in allowing them to purchase this special piece of land.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Big Cypress Plantation presents a unique opportunity for the conservation community to protect an ecologically significant forested wetland tract in the Four Hole Swamp Focus Area at bargain sale price. The property is located in Orangeburg Country, near Providence, SC. It consists of approximately 3.5 miles of bottomlands hardwoods associated with the Four Hole Swamp, an internationally-recognized habitat for avian and other wetland-dependent species. The conservation easement will prevent all commercial timber harvests in perpetuity, guaranteeing water quality and the natural integrity of the site in perpetuity.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Big Rock, within the Nine Times Forest in Pickens County, is South Carolina's most important and popular rock-climbing destination. The one acre access expansion will allow additional public access to this site.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Big Rock Public Access Tract is a unique and important climbing resource for South Carolina, and a significant area in the Southeastern region. Featuring high quality granite, it's a remarkably diverse climbing area. The cliff face provides many opportunities for the technical, roped climber, at any ability level. The boulder field below provides many fun and challenging opportunities for the boulderer. This area provides other great, low-impact recreational opportunities such as hiking and bird watching.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Big Snooks Tract is in the South Lowcountry Focus Area and consists of mature bottomland hardwood wetland associated with the Savannah River floodplain. The upland area consists of areas of mature mixed pine/hardwood. This property supports a wide variety of wildlife species and serves a vital role to improve water quality by providing for nutrient uptake, sediment deposition, and filtration from runoff draining from upstream lands.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This is a beautiful small valley farm managed for hunting and game in conjunction with several adjoining landowners. There are several historical rice field terraces compatible with pre-industrial era farming. Historical Indian artifacts are located near the Cherokee Trail. The tract has immediate development demands. It adjoins several other protected properties as well as the largest wetlands area in the region.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Black Creek Plantation is located in the ACE Basin Focus Area and has approximately 1.6 miles of direct Combahee River frontage with nearly 300 acres of bottomland hardwood wetland and blackwater braided streams associated with the Combahee River floodplain. The upland areas primarily consist of planted loblolly and slash pine stands, several agricultural fields and wildlife food plots.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Black River Landing Tract is comprised of 19 acres of upland pine habitat associated with the Black River watershed which is well-known for its rich wildlife habitat values, supporting the full spectrum of biodiversity from game species to threatened and endangered species. This tract is a critical addition to Rocky Point Community Forest and is the site of one of the historic ricefield plantations along the Black River.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_name: Black River State Park - Phase I
property_description: The Black River, stretching 150 miles exclusively within SC, is one of the most beautiful and under-utilized rivers in state with the potential to offer residents and visitors a wilderness-quality experience along a coastal-plain river. South Carolina Conservation Bank funding supports the acquisition of the 310-acre Phase I in Williamsburg County as part of a growing network of protected natural areas along the Black River and one of four properties targeted for the first phase of a unique riverine State Park in South Carolina. SC PRT and partners engaged in this project envision a network of State Park and additional public access holdings stretching 70 miles along the Black River which will create a unique experience for visitors, unlike any other park in SCPRT’s system.
notes: Part of SCPRT's Black River State Park
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_name: Black River State Park - Phase II
match_notes: Local: Butler Conservation Fund ($100,000), Knobloch Family Foundation ($350,000), George Leoning Foundation ($253,860) Federal: NCWCGP ($1,000,000) & NAWCA ($800,000)
property_description: The Black River, stretching 150 miles exclusively within SC, is one of the most beautiful and under-utilized rivers in the state with the potential to offer residents and visitors a wilderness-quality experience along a coastal-plain river. The 816-acre tract is a part of a growing network of protected natural areas along the Black River and a key acquisition for a new State Park in SC. The largely forested context of this coastal-plain river system makes it a unique and superior resource for SC contributing to wildlife habitat, water quality, flood mitigation, scenic, and recreational values of this treasured resource. This area is also known for its rich historical resources and numerous historical sites.
notes: Part of SCPRT's Black River State Park
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_name: Black River State Park - Phase III (RMS South Tract)
match_notes: Local: Butler Conservation Fund ($235,000), Knobloch Foundation ($735,530) Federal: NAWCA
property_description: The 738-acre acquisition includes 4.5 river miles of forested frontage on the SC Black Scenic River. This tract is part of a growing network of protected natural areas along the Black River and a key acquisition for a new State Park in South Carolina unline any other in SCPRT's system. Manages for public access, this project will offer access to the river itself as well as education, interpretation, and passive recreation opportunities on the lands along the river including fishing, boating, hiking, biking, camping, birding, nature exploration and education.
notes: Part of SCPRT's Black River State Park
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Black Swamp Plantation lies within the floodplain of the Savannah River. This tract is part of the Savannah River Preserve; a voluntary effort by landowners to preserve lands at a low cost of $200 an acre. This particular tract has tremendous water storage capacity, both above and below ground. Preservation of this land will help lesson the severity of downstream flooding.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Blackmon Tract represents the opportunity to add 150 acres to the Aiken Gopher Tortoise Heritage Preserve. The acquisition of this land gives the preserve much needed access to the South Edisto River. The Gopher Tortoise Preserve is home to the rare and state-listed endangered gopher tortoise, which provide shelter to many other species in their 30-foot long burrows which can be up to fifteen feet deep. The preserve is also home to one fifth of the state’s remaining longleaf pine/wiregrass communities. Along with the tortoises visitors can expect to see deer, wild turkey, quail, fox, barred owls, and red - tailed hawks, several varieties of snakes as well as the migrating great crested flycatchers and blue grosbeaks. The Blackmon Tract addition is open to the public for all pedestrian, equestrian and non-motorized vehicular uses.
notes: Part of SCDNR's Aiken Gopher Tortoise Heritage Preserve / Wildlife Management Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Blue Heron Property was in the core of the battlefield for the August 16, 1780, Battle of Camden. Major General Gates assembled his troops so that his most inexperienced men would face the most experienced British Regulars and vice versa. His decision is considered one of the worst tactical decisions made by an American during the war. As the battle wore on, the Patriot numbers dwindled and they would eventually be outnumbered 800 to 2,000. In the midst of the melee, DeKalb attempted to rally his men and was shot 11 times by musket fire. In one hour, the Americans were routed, suffering over 2,000 casualties. That evening, Gates mounted his horse and fled to Charlotte, NV. This, his most humiliating defeat, caused a loss of arms, men, and equipment that haunted the Americans for months. Gates never returned to military served. This property is the site of this last stand of American troops led by DeKalb.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This property has a .9 mile stretch of land on scenic Highway 11. It adjoins several other parcels of land that have previously received grants from the Bank. This tract is part of the face headlands of Caesar's Head where it has a significant view shed, and it also adjoins a state park and Mountain Bridge Passage.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Blythe-Goodwin House represents an extraordinary opportunity to preserve one of the finest examples of early architecture typical of the foothills region from the later part of the eighteenth century. This house, built in 1790 sits at the intersection of Scenic Highway 11 and US Highway 25. This house was purchased with funds made possible from the SC Conservation Bank, the County of Greenville, SCDOT and the Greenville Chapter of the Cherokee Foothills National Scenic Byway Association. The house is currently on The National Register of Historic Places. The house will be restored and turned into an Upcountry Museum. There is a side building on the property that will likewise be restored and converted into a welcome center for visitors to the area.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This is the first of two tracts located in Orangeburg County and will likely act as a lynchpin to promote further Conservation in this area. It sits between Neeses and Springfield in the Edisto Watershed. There are several ponds on the tract as well as historic pre-colonial sites.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Jack H. Boineau Tract is a historical site on Highway 174 in Adams Run, SC, that consists of 15.45 acres. This tract is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. This property was the first home site in the newly established summer village for St. Paul's Parish in 1830. The property was established as the headquarters for the Third Military District of South Carolina in 1861, and also was home to a Confederate hospital and a substantial ammunition depot during the war.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Boone Hall Plantation consists of nearly 600 acres in the heart of Mount Pleasant and abuts over 1.5 miles of Boone Hall Creek. The historic property features diverse ecosystems and wildlife habitat, and provides an oasis of natural land in the fast-growing region of Coastal South Carolina. The antebellum-era plantation is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and is open to the public for a variety of tourism, cultural, agricultural, and community events and activities. Boone Hall serves as an anchor greenspace property within the broader Lowcountry landscape.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Many of the tributaries that feed Lake Keowee are unprotects, contain rare and endangered species, are vulnerable to development, and pose a threat to the Lake Keowee watershed if they were developed in a damaging way. Boones Creek is also a critical habitat for the Oconee Bell, the signature species of the Jocassee and Keowee watersheds. The Boones Creek Oconee Bell Preserve has a population of thousands of flowering individuals and acts as a wildlife corridor for mammals, reptiles, and fishes.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Bowers Tract represents a key tract of land for the Savannah River Preserve program. The Savannah River Preserve represents a group of voluntary landowners who wish to place easements on their land for the low cost of $250 an acre. In this case the landowner placed the easement for the cost of $176 an acre. The Bowers tract is within the Savannah River watershed and contains over 135 acres of wetlands. The Conservation Bank contributed a mere 16% of the total value of the conservation easement.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Boyd Pond Tract was an opportunity for the Aiken County Open Land Trust to work with several entities to purchase 84 acres. This property is to be preserved in perpetuity as a natural area with full public access for outdoor recreation to include softball/soccer fields, fishing, picnicking, and hiking.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Steve Boyd Tract is a property in Chester County consisting of 1,000 acres of prime soil farm land under production in the unique and rare South Carolina Blackjacks. These soil series have high moisture holding capacity due to very slow permeability, and the ability to continue producing during short term droughts. This farm has been in agricultural production by the family for over 120 years. This property is a portion of a larger farm which has been farmed continuously by family members since 1882, and was placed in a conservation easement with Katawba Valley Land Trust.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Bramblewood Tract is managed for forestry and wildlife near the Wateree River with a diversity of habitats and forest areas including loblolly pine stands and hardwood riparian areas. Healthy populations of all major game species in South Carolina, including white-tailed deer and wild turkey. The property boarders the Wateree River and is located in the historic Camden District of Kershaw County.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

match_notes: Local: Easley Combined Utilities ($30,000) and ReWa ($20,000)
property_description: The Bramlett Bottoms property has historically been farmed in row crop plasticulture and during rain events dumps loads of harmful sediment, pesticides, herbicides and fungicides into the North Saluda River. Recent temperature data gathered by SCDNR fisheries biologists have revealed that bottom releases from the Poinsett Reservoir are cold enough to be able to sustain a breeding population of trout in this section of the river. The goal with this property is to move to a more sustainable farming practice, improve the riparian habitat along the river and work with SCDNR to implement instream restoration structures to create a catch-and-release fishery in this area of northern Greenville County.
notes: Part of SCDNR's Cedar Mountain Heritage Preserve
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Bryan Diary tract is located on Johns Island and has 3,000 feet of frontage along the Kiawah River. The owner of the land has agreed to place an easement on the property for one tenth of the fair market value. This is an excellent opportunity for the Conservation Bank to help preserve rural life on Johns Island.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Bugby Plantation is located on Wadmalaw Island outside of Charleston.This tract of land has 11,000 feet of frontage along Bohicket Creek. The landowner is donating two-thirds of the value of the conservation easement and Charleston Greenspace is providing matching Conservation Bank funds. Bugby Plantation is and will remain a working farm.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is located at the convergence of two creeks and is an important botanical tract with rare plants on the property. It will become a public park with hiking trails.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Burbage Farm is a magnificent parcel of relatively undeveloped property traversed by the braided streams of the Coosawhatchie River and Cowpen Creek in Hampton County. The property is currently used for hunting, timber, and agricultural activities. It is prominently visible by the public from Gray's Highway, having approximately 1,500 feet of scenic road frontage. Burbage Farm contains a diversity of relatively natural habitats including agricultural field, variously aged planted pine stands, mixed upland forest, forested wetlands, scrub-shrub bottomland, and hardwood swamp, all of which can support a variety of floral and faunal species.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Burgess Farms Tract contains contains a mixture of bottomland hardwoods along Boggy Swamp and a mixture of planted pine flatwood. The forest structure and access to water provides optimal shelter and forage habitat for white-tailed deer. The property borders Boggy Swamp which empties into the Scenic Black River four miles downstream. The property is enrolled in the Safe Harbor Program and a majority of the tract's soils are prime farmland.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The McRae property is part of the Conservation Bank’s continuing effort to preserve working farms facing increasing pressure from development. The Dillard Barn which is located on the property is used for curing tobacco and is on the National Register of Historic Places.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Kenny Cain's land is part of the Conservation Bank's ongoing effort to save small farms in South Carolina. Mr. Cain received matching funds from the Federal Ranch Land Protection Program. Thanks to these organizations this will continue to be a working family farm for future generations.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract has 2 miles of frontage on Cane Creek as well as two source creeks to a Fishing Creek. The property has a Heron Rookery on site. The tract will become part of the Greenway Preserve with high public access.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Cannon tract is part of the Cane Savannah Plantation established by Matthew Singleton in 1756 as a gift from the state for his services during the Revolutionary War. Emma Lee and Dale Cannon are committed to preserving this land from the encroaching sprawl of nearby Shaw Air Force Base and Sumter. The land is home to numerous wildlife including quail, turkey, songbirds, foxes, deer and bobcats. There is an active trophy management program for the thriving deer population and a forestry program for the mature hardwoods and pine which could support red-cockaded woodpeckers. This land is open to students for educational purposes.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Cantey Bay Tracts are managed for agriculture, forestry, and wildlife, within the "waterfowl corridor" of Lake Marion. A diversity of habitats and agricultural areas occur here, including many fields that are in food and fiber productions. This property may have been a part of the Native American civilization that inhabited and built the mound at Fort Watson nearby, and part of the history of human travel around the Santee River in historic times. One of the most significant aspects of this property is the fact that it is near some amazing public lands; Santee, Manchester State Forest, Lake Marion, and Congaree National Park. These tracts also have about 10 miles of road viewing and lie within 5 miles of several other conservation easements.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

match_notes: Local: $88,000 (OCCB) Private Donors: $13,000 Deficit: raise via other local outlets
property_description: The Chapman Bridge Oconee Bell Preseve builds on the McKinney Creek and Boones Creek Oconee Bell Preserves and Devils Fork State Park by protecting critical habitat and forest for the iconic Oconee Bell. The property contains prodigous populations of the plant, which is an umbrella species for myriad native flora and fauna of the Jocassee and Keowee watersheds and a marker of clean water, which feeds into a public drinking supply.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Chauga Bluff contains an estimated 2.5 miles of direct frontage on the Chauga River as well as at least nine tributaries to the Chauga River. This property includes headwaters that feed into Lake Hartwell, which provides drinking water to over 14 municipalities and over 190,000 people. There are also several small wetlands on the property and prime farmland soils. A historic cemetery is located on the site, with graves dating to the mid 1800s. While not extensively studied on this site, Native American activity in this general area and on sites such as Chauga Bluff is well documented.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Chauga Heights Tract will protect and make available 1 mile of frontage on the Chuaga River that connects the network of trails and campgrounds of Chau Ram Park. The Chauga River is a stunning world-class resource; its cold water moves over rapids and shallow shoals, offering opportunities for rafting, kayaking, and fishing. Currently, the Chau Ram Park sees over 40,000 visitors annually and routinely have to turn visitors away due to capacity issues in the summer. This property will expand its trail network and provide additional recreational opportunities along the river.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract adjoins a very well maintained city park and would be used as an extension on the other side of the paved road. The tract has over one mile of frontage on the important Chauga River and is located on the city water supply.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Chestnut Ridge Extension abuts the Chestnut Ridge Heritage Preserve and also connects to the Greenville Watershed and Blue Wall Preserve. The priority habitats/features occurring on this site include: Appalachian oak forest, cove forests, rock outcrops, and cataract bogs. Game species such as bear, deer, turkey, quail, ruffed grouse, spotted skunk and other furbearers abound. Unique finds on the property include 5 Eastern wood rat nets. Cultural resources on the property include arrowheads, flakes, and chert which have been found in an old roadbed. Outstanding views of Squirrel Mountain and Hogback Mountain can be viewed from the subject property, as well as their associated habitat features, which include cataract bogs, rock outcrops, springs and seeps.
notes: Part of SCDNR's Chestnut Ridge Heritage Preserve / Wildlife Management Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The 37 acres purchased with funds from the Conservation Bank were the first phase of a much needed greenway connecting I-85 and downtown Spartanburg. The greenway is an integral part of the Palmetto Trail and provides passive recreation opportunities to the residents of Spartanburg County. The Chinquapin Creek was part of Spartanburg County's first drinking water supply. Spartanburg Regional Healthcare systems provides $10,000 annually to the maintenance of the trail as it integrates beautifully with the Hospice House and Miliken Research Park.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is located in northern Beaufort County and is an important piece within the ACE Basin. This property is considered a linch pin for future easements. The tract is near several other properties with Bank grants. It has ten miles of frontage on the Whale Branch River and adjoins a state park while also containing a cattle farm and recreational park.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Cleveland Property and the Wilson Farms Property combine to form an extraordinary tract of land. This 867 acres is located on what the Cherokee Indians call the “Blue Wall.” It is an area where the Blue Ridge Mountains come to a precipitous end. This magnificent area is one of the wettest places in America containing 50 waterfalls and a habitat for 400 rare and endangered plant and animal species. The acquisition of this property helps ensure this area continues to be protected. The property directly adjoins Jones Gap Park, has 1.5 miles of river frontage along the Middle Saluda and contains the famous view “Pretty Place.” This marvelous piece of property was purchased in three separate phases between 2005 and 2007.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Comalander family tracts are managed for wildlife, agriculture and forestry with a diversity of habitats, including planted pine stands, pine-hardwood forest, cove hardwood forest, piedmont bottomland hardwood riverine forest, and food plots of cultivated or grass croplands fields. Healthy populations of all major game species in South Carolina, including white-tailed deer, wild turkey, waterfowl, and small game occur here. Also present are species of furbearers such as otter, beaver, mink, skunk, bobcat, raccoon, fox and black bear. The bottom lands along the river and creek areas are attractive to waterfowl species including wood duck and to a lesser extent other species of ducks such as mallards and black duck. Also along the river and creeks there may be wading birds and marsh birds and during dry period on may see wild turkey.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Combahatchie Family Tract is a magnificent piece of relatively undeveloped property on the braided streams of the Combahee River, the border of Colleton and Hampton Counties. The property is currently used for hunting, timber and agricultural activities. It is prominently visible by the public from Lowcountry Highway, having approximately 2500 feet of scenic road frontage. This property lies within the ACE Basin Focus Area featuring diverse ecosystems and a wealth of wildlife. Combahatchie is in close proximity to several other protected lands.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is located in the Cowassee Basin on the Wateree "Blue Trail." The property has 5.8 miles of frontage on the Wateree River and 2.7 miles on Beech Creek. The landowner will allow public boat-in camping in designated areas along the Wateree River "Blue Trail."
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Cope Tract is a parcel of land primarily comprised of regenerating hardwood forests on the Little Salkehatchie River. The property is currently used for hunting, timber and agricultural activities. It is prominently visible by the public from Shiloh Loop, having approximately 1,900 feet of road frontage. Cope Tract lies within the nearly 1.7 million acres of the Ashepoo, Combahee, and Edisto (ACE) Basin Focus Area and contains a diversity of relatively natural habitats including planted pine stands, upland pine, forested wetlands, open areas, and regenerating wetlands, all of which can support a variety of floral and faunal species. Cope Tract lies within the floodplain of the Little Salkehatchie that flows into the Combahee River, leading into the St. Helena Sound, and is within the Broad - St. Helena Watershed. This tract is also located in close proximity to other protected lands.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This is a forested tract with 96 acres of wetlands that is part of the SOLO Project. It is adjacent to the Hamilton Ridge tract. There are efforts to restore longleaf pines on the tract, and the streams on the property connect to the Savannah river which is important for water quality.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Cordova Road tract is surrounded by development and is located just West of the City of Orangeburg.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract has 3.85 miles of frontage on the Coosawhatchie River as well as land bordering I-95. The tract has 872 acres of fresh and brackish water, forested woodlands, and several miles of marsh at one point on both sides of the river.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Cotton Hills Farm is one of the top ecotourism destinations in South Carolina. Located along two creeks that flow into the Broad River, Cotton Hills is a working family farm. The farm rests on a ridge whose altitude allows for cooler temperatures in which peaches thrive. The farm also contains the preservation of Blackjack Soils, the last remnants of the prairie that once covered South Carolina. Cotton Hills Farm has many agricultural based educational opportunities. The farm is in the ever-expanding Charlotte metro region and thus was in danger of development before Conservation Bank funds helped secure its future.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Crab Orchard Plantation is part of the Savannah River Conservation Program. The Program is a voluntary effort by landowners to preserve lands along the Savannah River. The Crab Orchard tract has 3.5 miles of frontage along the Savannah River. The tract also has wetlands and bottomland hardwood forests.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Cragmoor Farms contains significant plant and wildlife habitat associated with mesic deciduous forest, Piedmont bottomland forest, narrow stream valley forest, and cultivated land. The property shares a border of 825 linear feet with Still House Branch, a tributary of the North Tyger River. This land and more surrounding was acquired by Charles Moore beginning with a purchase in 1762. The property is currently leased for fescue hay production, soybeans, feed grains, and wheat in the winter. Spartanburg School District Six is committed to giving children hands-on learning experiences with farming, forestry, environmental protection and conservation, biology, ecology, and history, and then serving the healthy foods they produce in their cafeterias. This property is an ideal location for these programs that are keeping with a national trend to combat such epidemics such as childhood obesity and hunger with a movement toward increase local food in schools.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Creek Farms property has 77.7 acres of forested land on Edisto Island. This magnificent piece of land has acres of live oak trees, wetlands and woodlands. The property also has significant frontage along Highway 174. The market value for this land if it was sold and subdivided into the 27 allowable lots would be $3,695,000. The Conservation Bank contributed a small fraction of the easement value.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Heritage Tract is unique in that it combines significant natural resource values with extensive varieties of cultural and historical values. From a natural resources standpoint, the Heritage Tract is 2,000 acres surrounding the Great Falls of the Catawba River. This land includes 300 acres of bottomland riparian hardwood forests with an average age of 120 years old. The tract also contains 550 acres of gently rolling upland forests. From a historical perspective, the tract was the site of several Revolutionary War battles, a Federal Arsenal established in 1802 by President Thomas Jefferson, several turn of the century hydro-electric dams and the resulting historic town of Great Falls. The Heritage Tract is also significant in that having 2,000 preserved acres so close to urban Charlotte and Rock Hill will provide the residents of these areas with protected lands and recreational opportunities. Among these opportunities are proposed bike trails under the Federal Rails to Trails program.
notes: Part of SCDNR's Catawba River Wildlife Management Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Crescent Tract lies within the more than 2 millions acres of the South Lowcountry (SoLo) Focus Area featuring diverse ecosystems and a wealth of wildlife. This tract contains a diversity of relatively natural habitats including upland pine forest and forested wetlands in various stages of succession, and open field, all of which can support a variety of floral and faunal species. Protection of Crescent Tract presents an opportunity to contribute to the protection of the downstream water quality for the benefit of the public.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The William Crosby Tract will be usedfor agricultural activities on his property to provide educational opportunities for students. The landowner is particularly interested in working with local chapters of the Future Farmers of America, 4-H Clubs and similar youth groups to provide opportunities to visit his farm and gain "hands-on" experience in agriculture. This property includes approximately 38 acres of forested lands where mostly natural mixed hardwoods are found and 69 acres of open land. The open area is used for various activities such as hay production and fenced pastures for cattle. A small perennial stream flows through the forested portion about 790 feet.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is part of the SOLO program. It has 2.17 miles of frontage on the Little Salkehatchi and Upper Combahee Rivers, and it is part of the ACE Basin. The area is publically used for a paddling trail.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Culbertson Mill is an incredible scenic, historic, agricultural and natural resource in Laurens County, SC. This divers and remarkable property has long been enjoyed by the public as a recreational resource. Known as Ekom Beach to locals, generations of family have hunted, fished, and gone swimming there. This property contains approximately 3,290 feet of frontage along the Reedy River, 1,830 feet of frontage on Ekom Beach Road, and 30 acres of prime and important soils. Culbertson Mill's diverse timber stands, river frontage, connectivity to other undeveloped land, and mix of open field and cover make it ideal habitat for a diverse array of wildlife.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service
SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Cypress Creek tracts of land are part of the Savannah River Preserve. This land represents a volunteer effort by landowners along the Savannah River to protect vast amounts of land at the greatly reduced price of $250 an acre. This particular tract consists of pine and hardwood river bottom along the Cypress Creek, a tributary to the Savannah River. This tract borders on Two Sisters Ferry Road, dating back to the 1700's, which served as a strategic route across the Savannah River during the Revolutionary War.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Cypress Creek tracts of land are part of the Savannah River Preserve. This land represents a volunteer effort by landowners along the Savannah River to protect vast amounts of land at the greatly reduced price of $250 an acre. This particular tract consists of pine and hardwood river bottom along the Cypress Creek, a tributary to the Savannah River. This tract borders on Two Sisters Ferry Road, dating back to the 1700's, which served as a strategic route across the Savannah River during the Revolutionary War.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Cypress Swamp is within the nearly 1.7 million acres of the Ashepoo, Combahee, and Edisto (ACE) Basin Focus Area featuring diverse ecosystems and a wealth of wildlife. This property contains a diversity of relatively natural habitats including forested and non-forested wetlands, all of which can support a variety of floral and faunal species. Protection of Cypress Swamp presents an opportunity to contribute to the protection of the downstream water quality for the benefit of the public. Bisected by U.S. Interstate I-26, this property has approximately 2,000 feet of scenic frontage along either side of the interstate for the benefit of the public.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This is an historic property listed on the National Historic Register. The landowner will receive matching funds from the Federal Ranch land Protection Program. The land contains an historical home site and prime farmland. Prior to securing funds from the Conservation Bank, the owner had been approached by several interested parties for subdivision and development of the property.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Dawn Plantation is located in the ACE Basin Focus Area. It was established in 1791 on the banks of the Ashepoo River as a working plantation, with rice production being one of its primary crops. The property has approximately 2.5 miles of direct Ashepoo River frontage with over 200 acres of various type wetland habitats. The upland areas primarily consist of stands of mixed pine/hardwoods, open fields, planted longleaf and loblolly pine stands, agricultural fields and wildlife food plots.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract has 3.5 miles of frontage on Spears Creek and .31 mile on the Wateree River.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract borders Lake Marion on Cantey Bay with .33 miles of frontage. It adjoins the Santee National Wildlife Refuge and the landowner has plans to build waterfowl impoundments.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Deer Park lies within the more than 2 million acres for the South Lowcountry Focus Area featuring diverse ecosystems and a wealth of wildlife. This tract contains a diversity of relatively natural habitats including upland pine forest and forested wetlands in various stages of succession, and open fields, all of which can support a variety of floral and faunal species. These natural habitats are significant to wildlife habitat functions for migratory songbirds and ground-nesting birds, waterfowl and other avian species, game and non-game mammals of various sizes, as well as for amphibians and reptiles. Protection of Deer Park presents an opportunity to contribute to the protection of the downstream water quality for the benefit of the public.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: DeLoach Farm is within the more than 2 million acres of the South Lowcountry (SoLo) Focus Area featuring diverse ecosystems and a wealth of wildlife. This tract contains a diversity of relatively natural habitats including variously aged planted and natural pine stands, mixed upland forested and non-forested wetlands, open areas and open groves, all of which can support a variety of floral and faunal species. DeLoach Farm is located on Sanders Branch and House Fork, as well as Coosawhatchie River, which leads into the Broad River and Port Royal Sound, and is within the Broad - St. Helena Watershded. This property is situated on and prominently visible by the public from Hickory Hill Road, having over 2 miles of scenic frontage, as well as Pocotaligo Road, having over 1 mile of scenic frontage along both sides of the road.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Located in the high hills of Santee, the Cowassee Basin, and the Wateree rivershed, this tract is home to a confederate burial grounds and a historic Native American location dating back to the Revolutionary War. Mill Pond, a 165 acre lake on the property, was established for colonial commerce in 1732.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Dixon Family Tracts consists of four different parcels in Williamsburg County that total 535 acres of forested lands, cleared/open lands, and wetlands. These tracts are managed for forestry and wildlife near Black Mingo Creek. There are bottomlands along Black Mingo Creek and Poplar Hill Branch. A diversity of habitats and forest areas occur here, including loblolly pine stands, mixed pine hardwoods, creek and stream bottomland hardwoods and small wildlife food agriculture fields. Several species of major game, birds, amphibians, and reptiles can be found on these tracts throughout the year. These properties may have had Native American camps as a Native American Village was located near all the tracts and became the town called Indiantown. The Dixon family purchased these tracts around 1930, and have been in the family ever since.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Donoho Farm is a working family farm totaling in 2,055 acres of agricultural and wooded property, with associated farm and residential structures. This property is located primarily along South Carolina Highway 9, approximately 2.3 miles southeast of Clio, SC, on the Dillon County/Marlboro County Line. The Donoho Farm is a diverse property with creek frontage, cropland, pasture, and woodlands along with a 592 acre Carolina Bay. The landowner donated 50% of the easement value.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Douglas B. Sheorn property is characterized by stands of planted pine, mixed hardwoods, wildlife openings, and bottomland hardwoods. The property has significant elevation changes, rising sharply from the floodplain of Beaver Creek to hilltops that offer sweeping vistas of the Beaver Creak drainage south and the Stonboro/Liberty Hill are to the northwest. Managed forest lands surround the property and adjacent tract are primarily recreational hunting lands. The primary use of the Sheorn property is for the recreation with the primary activities game management and hunting.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Eddie Drayton Tract is 670 acres in Marlboro County with a large portion being forested land and wetlands. On the property there is also about 28 acres of cleared or open lands, a 24 acre Henegan Lake, 1.1 miles of the Muddy Creek that runs through the property, and 1.25 miles of frontage on the Great Pee Dee River.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The 121-acre DuRant Farm project presents a unique opportunity for the conservation community to protect an ecologically rich and agriculturally significant tract of land at a bargain sail price. The property is located near Hemingway, SC and is an extremely well-managed, productive small farm that provides habitat for numerous game and non-game species alike. It contains a variety of land features, including mature bottomland hardwood forest, productive agricultural fields, pollinator plots and a small pond that attracts migratory waterfowl. Approximately 1/2 miles of Hughes Branch meanders along its southern boundary. As a 3rd generation farm, the landowner's primary goal is to ensure that it remains in productive agricultural, timber and recreational use by putting it under a conservation easement. Once conserved, the owner hoped to establish a "you pick" farm that will be seasonally open to the public.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Dusty Acres Tract is located in the Santee Waterfowl Corridor and borders a SCDNR WMA in Clarendon County. The tract is comprised of farmland and has managed waterfowl impoundments.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Edward Hickson Tract is 318 acres of land in Georgetown County between the towns of Georgetown and Hemingway. This land has considerable frontage on Pittman Creek. Aside from the natural beauty of the land, the tract has considerable historical value as well. During the Civil War, Francis Marion used the land to as a base for his horses and troops to use during his many famous raids on the enemies. There was a house on the land that was on The National Register of Historic Places until it was unfortunately destroyed by a fire in 1980.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Edisto Packers Tract is dominated by South Atlantic inland maritime forest and intertidal marsh communities. The tract is adjacent to the ACE Basin and provides a significant linkage between the ACE Basin and the Toogoodoo Creek.The value of this land rests not only its beauty but its magnificent habitat to a variety of species. This land is perhaps most important for its American wintering grounds of many Caribbean and Latin American neotropical migratory birds. Conservation of this land will also assist in the long term conservation of the Bald Eagle, the wood stork and the shortnose sturgeon. The purchase of this land contributes to the already preserved 1,618,767 acres of the ACE Basin.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This magnificent piece of property is contiguous with the 13,000 acre Francis Beidler Forest. The forest is home to one of the largest remaining stands of bald cypress and tupelo gum trees in the world. This area is currently used by two private hunt clubs that lease the rights to deer and hog hunting to 1,000 people a day during hunting season. When not in hunting season, the property is used for natural history education courses conducted by the Audubon Society. The area also has many trails for hiking and biking. Other land uses include scientific research, environmental education courses taught by surrounding schools, wildlife observation, canoeing as well as hunting and fishing.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is a SOLO Preserve transaction, and the tract consists of two separate pieces of property located close to each other. It contains a Carolina Bay and acts as a long leaf pine community. The Elliott tract adjoins other grants that were previously made by the Bank.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Exley Plantation tract was one of the five largest tracts left unprotected in the SOLO area. This grant ensures the water quality of the Savannah River to remain undisturbed in this area. The tract borders 1.1 miles of the Savannah River and is adjacent to the Beaufort-Jasper Water Authority intake as well as across the river from the Savannah River National Wildlife Refuge and the Webb Wildlife Center.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The McCrady/Fairfield Tract is managed for forestry and wildlife near the US Sumter National Forest with a diversity of habitats and forest areas including loblolly pine stands and hardwood ravine areas. Healthy populations of all major game species in SC, including white-tailed deer and wild turkey. This tract is located above the fall line in the lower Piedmont region and rolling hills of Fairfield County which support listed landscapes such as the cove / ravine oak-hickory forest ecosystems and such areas support special communities of flora and fauna. This property offers public viewing opportunities by virtue of having road frontage alone Dave Jenkins Road which adds significantly to the scenic values enjoyed by the public enjoying recreational activities along the road.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract of land is located off of Scenic Highway 11 on the Chatooga Ridge. Fall Creek bisects this property and empties into the Chatooga River which has been rated a Top 10 Whitewater River in the US. There is an old gristmill on the property, dating back to the early 1900's. This piece of property represents a significant inholding in the Sumter National Forest, and upon acquisition became part of the National Forest. The owner was willing to donate 75% of fair market value to the easement. There will be limited public access to the mill site for historic tours.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract in Sumter County has 1.8 miles of frontage on the Wateree River, 2 miles on Beech Creek, and 3.48 miles on the Palmetto Trail. The tract will include a 300' buffer on all creeks, lakes, and roads. The landowner is allowing boat-in camping in designated areas along the Wateree River "Blue Trail."
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This large tract is located on historic Kings HWY in the Cowassee Basin and Santee Waterfowl Corridor. This is a working farm that contains a Carolina Bay, waterfowl impoundments totaling 200 acres, and timber and agricultural lands. This tract is important for the public access hunting program and the landowner has agreed to provide access to the public through draw hunts.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_name: First Citizens Bank/Back Swamp School Tr
property_description: This is one of two grants located in Florence County. Located just off I-95, the tract will become an educational park/nature preserve adjoining the school house built around the 1920s.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract of land near Sandhills State Forest represents a key acquisition from a public access standpoint. The Floyd Tract is next to McBee Wildlife Management Area (WMA) and unites three parcels together. The McBee WMA is managed for traditional outdoor recreation opportunities for the public. This area is also significant for longleaf restoration potential and for providing a buffer for Mill Creek, a key tributary to Lynches River. With proper management this area can be a protected habitat for the endangered red cockaded woodpecker.
notes: Part of SCDNR's McBee Wildlife Management Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The For Duck Tract is 193.75 acres in Clarendon County that consists of cleared/open lands, forests, and wetlands. This tract is managed for forestry and wildlife, and within the "waterfowl corridor" of Lake Marion. A diversity of habitats and forest areas occur here, including mature loblolly pine stands, mixed pine-hardwoods. This property attracts several varieties of major game species, waterfowl species, migratory birds, as well as reptiles and amphibians.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The picture above is taken on Lake Conestee of which the uplands and wetlands of the Forrester Property are intimately tied. Along with properties obtained under the Henderson Conestee tract, these lands provide habitat for a wide variety of terrestrial and avian species. These properties also provide a critical migration corridor for many songbirds. The acquisition of this property provides the last road frontage necessary to connect Lake Conestee and the Henderson farm tract.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Fort Pemberton project contains forested area which is second or third growth forest, regenerating naturally following the Civil War. Much of the wooded area encompasses the earthworks that make up the fort. The Spartina marshlands along the 270 linear feet of frontage on the Stono River amount to approximately 0.25-acres of marsh/riparian zone. The Fort Pemberton site is a unique feature in the history and was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Forty Acre Rock is part of the Flat Creek Heritage Preserve. The area has been a popular recreation spot for years, but had become abused and was in desperate need of management before the Conservation Bank came to the rescue. Along with funds from The Nature Conservancy, South Carolina Department of Natural Resources, The Cooperative Endangered Species Conservation Fund and the Conservation Bank this area will be preserved for years to come. Flat Creek is a major tributary into the Lynches River in Lancaster which supports one of the healthiest populations of the Carolina Heelsplitter, a federally endangered species. The acquisition of Forty Acre Rock will increase the buffer along Flat Creek from 1.9 miles to 4.6 miles.
notes: Part of SCDNR's Forty Acre Rock Heritage Preserve and Wildlife Management Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Fox Tindal Farm Tract is 199.56 acres consisting of mostly cleared or open lands with a small portion of forested lands and wetlands in Clarendon County. This tract is managed for forestry and wildlife near the COWSSE Basin area and within the "waterfowl corridor" of Lake Marion. A diversity of habitats and forest areas occur here, including loblolly pine stands, mixed pine-hardwoods and agriculture fields. These natural habitats help several species of birds, mammals, reptiles, and amphibians thrive. There are also bottom lands along Big Branch Creek.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Sosnowski property is located on Wadmalaw Island, outside of Charleston. Mr. Sosnowski owns four separate properties representing an historic opportunity to protect deep water property on a sea island where development of the land could bring fair market value in excess of $50,000,000.00.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: French Quarter Creek is located on US Highway 41 in Huger, SC, within the Cooper River watershed and within the proclamation boundary of the Francis Marion National Forest. This property contains forested wetlands, which function to improve water quality by providing for nutrient uptake and sediment deposition from runoff draining from upstream lands, and also provides many wildlife habitat components. French Quarter Creek is located in close proximity to other protected properties. The protection of this tract extends the protective network and corridors that these surrounding private protected and public lands provide to diverse populations of plants and animals.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is in Moncks Corner and is surrounded by development. It is a historic Revolutionary War site with a British Fort. It adjoins Old Santee Canal Park and has 3,500 feet of frontage on Cedar Creek.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Gap Creek Project encompasses one of the largest properties in single ownership left unprotected in the SC Mountains. This is a keystone project for connecting over 40,000 acres of mountain lands from Table Rock Watershed to the North Saluda Watershed, known as the Mountain Bridge Wilderness Area. Game species associated with these lands include black bear, wild turkey, bobcat, and even Ruffed grouse. The property harbors an extensive forest system and flowing from them is a series of headwater streams of the Saluda River Basin proving multiple cascades and small waterfalls. Water flowing from Gap Creeks lands will end up in the Saluda Lake, a recreational lake which also supplies the drinking water to the town of Easley, South Carolina. Currently a Wildlife Management Agreement with the SCDNR is held on the land so public hunting is available on properties. Once completed, this property is also expected to have full open access for hiking and other passive recreation available.
notes: Part of SCPRT's Mountain Bridge Wilderness Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is a typical small family farm in the Oconee farm outreach program. It consists of 65% prime soils and adjoins the previously accepted Tokeena Bank grant. The tract is a small farm that includes cattle, timber, and various crops.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Geddings Tract contains wetland forest, open shallow pond, edge areas between agricultural fields and is adjacent to Manchester State Forest.
notes: Part of SCFC's Manchester State Forest
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Gill Creek Preserve is located just outside the town of Lowndesville in Abbeville County, east of the Rocky River off Hwy 81. This property consists primarily of pine and hardwood forestland with minor frontage on Gill Creek. The property is home to a diverse array of wildlife including white-tailed deer, beaver, turkey, grey and red fox, bobcats, coyotes, hogs, and black bear. Located 1 mile north of the Little River - Savannah Focus Area, an area identified by Upstate Forever as an area that greatly contributes to water quality. The property contributes to the drinking water supply of Abbeville County from the Savannah River and Richard Russel Lake, the sole source utilized as drinking water. One acre of public access is provided adjacent to Old Rocky River Presbyterian Cemetery, which dates back to the 1700's. Access will be available from 7am until 7pm every day of the year. Notification of landowner is required. Contact Upstate Forever for more information.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is part of the SOLO Project in the lowcountry of South Carolina. The land has diverse timber and 797 acres of "old rice fields" which add to its' historical value. Historically, this tract was a timber tract, but it has recently been reclaimed and has some managed waterfowl areas.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Gopher Wood tract has been excellently managed as a working forest, wildlife habitat, and an outdoor recreational tract. The property is located within the Lower Coosawhatchie River watershed. This land is highly diverse and the uplands are comprised of planted pine, natural pine, mixed pine hardwood, and hardwood forest types. Gopher Wood provides foraging and breeding habitat for many game wildlife species including white-tailed deer, turkey, waterfowl, and bobwhite quail. The landowner installed 15 food plots throughout the property. The duck ponds also attract many different species of duck, but also provide wonderful habitat for other wetland loving birds.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is located in the ACE Basin and adjoins other protected lands. The property has 320 acres of historic rice fields and a 191 acre impoundment on Sandy Dam Creek.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Grant Meadow Addition is a meadow and forest tract at the base of Table Rock State Park and is one of the most significant properties in the Upstate. It sits along the north side of the Cherokee Foothills Scenic Highway and encompasses the spectacular view of the park's 1000-ft granite monolith from the road. The "Table Rock" itself is key to the Upstate's cultural heritage and sense of place.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract adjoins a state park and is located on the Cherokee Foothills scenic Byway. The tract has a viewshed of Table Rock and a pull off for viewing located directly across from Table Rock. This is an iconic spot in South Carolina that offers a view of the Blue Ridge escarpment and is a breathtaking tourist attraction.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Grassy Knob Tract is the first mountain in the southern viewshed when standing atop the famous Table Rock, one of SC's most popular state parks. This property boasts significant hardwoods, streams, and ideal habitat for deer, black bear, wild turkey, and many species of birds. Table Mountain Pine inhabits the high ridge of the property and in the spring, dozens of rare flowering orchids and plants bloom in the cove forests. This tract also contains the headwaters for North Fork Twelvemile Creek as well as a major tributary to the Oolenoy River. Grassy Knob is an ideal property for recreation such as hiking, hunting, mountain biking and horseback riding.
notes: Part of SCDNR's Grassy Knob Wildlife Management Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Great Falls area is considered one of the crown jewels of the Catawba River. It is an undeveloped, pristine area, halfway between urbanized Charlotte and Columbia. Several tracts of land have been purchased and will be managed by the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources for total public access for South Carolinians. A state park is planned which will encompass five islands along the river, created when the Catawba was originally dammed. There will be boundless opportunities for hiking, biking, kayaking and canoeing. The land is also a haven for many species of birds, including osprey, eagles, herons, egrets and vultures. Conservation Bank funds were instrumental in preserving this special place for both man and nature.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Green Mountain tract is a public park in Greenville that adjoins the Jones Gap State Park. This tract has 1/3 mile frontage on Oil Camp Creek near Middle Saluda River.
