property_description: Greenbrier Farms is a working farm located in Pickens County near Dacusville, SC. Joyce and John Palmer operate this 300 acre farm supplying herbicide and pesticide free natural meats to local markets. The Palmers have agreed to donate 50% of the value of the easement. The Conservation Bank has an interest in this land as it is a working farm with an economically viable future, but is also at risk of development.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Greenfield Plantation Corner is located in the Plantersville Historic District along the scenic Black River in Georgetown County, one of five principal rivers comprising the world-class Winyah Bay watershed. This property is known for its rich wildlife habitat values supporting the full spectrum of biodiversity from game species to threatened and endangered species. Although this property is only 1.53 acres, it contributes to the intrinsic rural, historical, and ecological values of this protected landscape.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Grey Logs Property has been a property of highest interest for the South Carolina State Park Service for several years. The property was split into 8 parcels almost a decade ago containing 6 residential lots. State Parks and conservation interests have been hoping to recombine those lots into one property and add that property to Caesar's Head State Park. This property will allow the State Park Service to add a parking lot to the property which in turn accomplishes several conservation goals: Safety - the current parking lot for the hiking trails in the area is limited to less than 20 cars. On busy weekends at Caesar's Head the parking lot fills leading to cars parking on both sides of Highway 276, presenting significant safety concerns for the public and the Park; Habitat Protection - decades ago the current trail heading towards Jones Gap from the current parking lot was placed in an area with many Threatened and Endangered Species. The trail will be re-routed to the new parking lot, preserving the area of T&E species. The old trail would be closed further protecting at least one species that is known in no other place; Better Access - A larger parking area would allow for better access to the entire Mountain Bridge especially for hikers and backpackers. The western side of Jones Gap State Park would especially benefit from having better trail access.
notes: Part of SCPRT's Mountain Bridge Wilderness Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Groton Uplands property supports some of the highest quality pine-savannah forests in the Southeast and associated plant and wildlife species. The 1,600+ acres of wetlands scattered throughout the uplands, coupled with the routine use of prescribed fire, results in a complex matrix of high-quality, intertwining native habitats. These diverse habitats support deer, turkey, and wild quail as well as populations of nongame species. The property is in one of DNR' s quail restoration focus areas. The pine savannah uplands are ranked highly for grassland birds like red-cockaded woodpeckers and Bachman's sparrows. Groton has been identified as containing important amphibian habitat, with the entire property being in the Southern Savannah River Valley Priority Amphibian and Reptile Conservation Area (PARCA). Groton's forests also buffer the adjacent Savannah River, where two imperiled aquatic mussels occur near the property.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This family farm, commonly known as Pine Hill, has been operated by the Edens family for generations and is currently farmed by Mr. Edens and his three sons. The farm is located in Dalzell, about 7 miles outside of Sumter. The 677.22 acres is primarily planted with corn, beans and peanuts. The home place on the property dates back to the 1700’s and is listed on The National Register of Historic Places. Before acquisition by the Conservation Bank, the property was at risk to development out of the military base in Sumter. The USDA's Farm and Ranch Land Protection Program allocated a grant for 50% of the value of the land. The Edens' allow groups of school children to visit the farm to see not only how a farm works, but also the undisturbed Carolina Bay which is present on the property.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Halidon Hill Plantation represents an important tract in Berkeley County that is similar to many of the SOLO tracts the Bank currently holds. It adjoins the Francis Marion Forest and other protected areas. 110 acres of this tract are controlled rice fields that benefit from the .3 miles of frontage on the East Cooper River.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Hamilton Ridge has been described as the type of property the South Carolina Conservation Bank was designed to protect. Hamilton Ridge is exceptional in size and natural resources as well as location. With 8.5 miles of river frontage along the Savannah River, this tract of land will provide many opportunities for fishing and outdoor recreation. This tract also provides habitat for several threatened or endangered species such as robust redhorses, woodstorks and bald eagles, although no formal study of these species has been conducted. Opportunities for extensive longleaf pine restoration also exist on this property. Before acquisition, this tract of land was in eminent danger of development. Hamilton Ridge is within 30 miles of quickly expanding Hardeeville and within one hour of Savannah, Georgia. International Paper, the former owner, agreed to work with the various conservation groups to ensure the future of this magnificent piece of property would not be subdivided and paved over.
notes: Part of SCDNR's Hamilton Ridge Wildlife Management Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Hanahan Tract totals 91 acres, most of which is tidal (Spartina) marsh. The remaining acreage consists of remnant maritime forest and upland species. A majority of the uplands were logged in 2012, resulting in the natural regeneration of sweetgum, oak, and pine species to a shrub-scrub stage. The property is strategically located in a priority conservation area known as the ACE Basin which is a National Estuarine Research Reserve and benefits innumerable waterfowl, wading birds, herpetofauna, migratory songbirds, and game species.
notes: Part of SCDNR's Bear Island Wildlife Management Area

property_description: Hickory Hills is a 315-acre, immaculately-managed hunting property located just outside the small town of Jonesville, SC. This property has approximately 290 acres of forested land cover, 12,000 feet of streams, 80 acres of wetlands, and a 7-acre fluctuating duck pond. These features benefit water quality and contribute to the wildlife diversity of the property. Hickory Hills part of land once owned by General James Means and his family. Members of the Means family served as soldiers and generals in the Revolutionary War, the War of 1812 and the Civil War. Structures associated with the historical Means House located on an adjacent tract still stand on this property, including slave quarters and barns.

source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Hopewell Church Property in the Pageland community contains the battlefield for the Battle of Waxhaws (aka Buford's Massacre). The battle was fought between Continental Army troops from Virginia led by Colonel Abraham Buford and a British Loyalist force led by Lt. Colonel Banastre Tarleton. While the unique and significant history of the property is the overwhelmingly compelling reason for the preservation of the site, there are other important conservation goals of this project. The conservation of this tract preserves important green space on a busy intersections that is rapidly developing in Lancaster County. The public will have year-round unfettered access to the property. The SCBPT intends to establish the property as a public park to interpret the Battle of Waxhaws and allow passive recreational use of the site.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

Acquisition of this tract gives the public access to previously inaccessible portions of the trail. This tract has 4000' along Long Cane Creek and 2000' along Mountain Creek. The Nature Conservancy was able to convince the current owner not to develop and with assistance from the Conservation Bank, funds were secured to preserve this property forever.

property_description: Indigo Farms consists of 6 separate parcels for a total of 102 acres. The property contains forested and cleared areas with scattered wetlands areas of less than one acre. Highway 174 is a South Carolina Scenic Highway that had been recommended for designation as a National Scenic By-Way. This scenic, rural waterfront farm is in one of the few remaining agricultural preservation areas designated for protection by the Charleston County Comprehensive Plan. It is in the only portion of Charleston County within the ACE Basin. It adjoins several other conserved properties in the northern part of Edisto Island.

Johns Properties I and II are located on Old Orangeburg Road near Garnett, SC. The property is primarily used for timber production and recreational use.  While providing significant conservation value on its own, the property is located in a neighborhood which presents excellent opportunity to build on landscape-scale conservation.  The property is surrounded by other large undeveloped tracts which link it to a conglomerate of other privately protected and publicly owned lands totaling over 50,000 contiguous acres.  The property contains significant forested wetlands which will be protected as preserves and over 3 miles of primarily forested road frontage which will be protected with a 300-foot setback buffer.  The property will be maintained as a working forest and utilized for agricultural production, recreational use and limited rural residential use, while permanently protecting the significant public benefits it provides.

The Conservation Bank was able to assist The Trust for Public in the acquisition of these special places. Johnson's Creek Camp will be turned over to South Carolina State Parks to be managed in conjunction with Hunting Island State Park. These magnificent pieces of property will be preserved as a natural resource and for educational purposes.

The quiet and lush corridor along Gap Creek, bordered by a canopied mountains provides a respite from summer temperatures and leads to an array of unique mountain flora, fauna and vistas that decades ago, inspired the creation of Jones Gap State Park. property_description: This Jones family's land is located along the Black River in the Pee Dee area. This magnificent piece of property fits tightly into a mosaic of protected properties in the immediate vicinity. By contributing to the existing protected lands, preservation of the Jones' tract reduces the threat of fragmentation, which would destroy habitat and reduce the functionality of the river. Non-fragmented lands are especially important for the Threatened Swallow-Tailed Kite, which has been spotted flying overhead. Funds from the Conservation Bank were instrumental in preserving this special place.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: JRJ Farms is ranked as a priority target for the Readiness and Environmental Protection Integration program given its proximity to the Joint-Base Charleston’s North Auxiliary Airfield (NAAF). The easement protects the unique upland pine forests and forested wetlands situated along the North Fork Edisto River (NFER). The protection of this property will serve as a critical wildlife corridor, preserve intact riparian habitat, and remove the threat of encroachment impacts on NAAF. The property consists of 120-acres comprised of mostly mixed pine-hardwood forests, forested wetlands, and wildlife openings along 1.2 miles of the NFER. Protection of this tract will preserve a 45-acre buffer of forested wetlands along the NFER, 68-acres of planted pine and mixed hardwoods, 2-acres of planted wildlife openings.The property is primarily managed for waterfowl, white-tailed deer, and wild turkeys. In addition, the property contains extensive forested wetlands providing habitat for a variety of birds, mammals, reptiles, and amphibians as well as providing scenic views to the public along the NFER. In addition, these wetlands protect water quality for the NFER which provides aquatic habitat for many rare fish including the Lowland Shiner and Blackbanded Sunfish. Protection of JRJ Farms adds to a variety of notable public parks and protected landscapes.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The 154-acre Keowee Extension tract occupies nearly a mile of frontage along the Cherokee Foothills National Scenic Highway in Pickens County. This property borders Keowee State Park on the western edge and Jocassee Gorge Wilderness Area to the east. Tucked away behind the road, the property is teeming with black bear and whitetail deer, which forage on the Skinned Pine Ridge and down through the watershed until reaching Little Eastatoee Creek. Large boulders and granite outcroppings offer refuge for large mammals and several den sites for black bear have been identified.

property_description: Keithfield is a farm and forest located in Spartanburg County in Pauline, SC. Earlier in its history, Keithfield was a site of significant Native American activity, as evidenced by the arrowheads frequently discovered in its fields. Limited public access is permitted on the property, and will continue to be offered to groups such as Boy Scouts, Young Life Leaders, and other church functions.

property_description: Protection of this large and wonderfully position property contributes greatly to the Francis Beidler Forest and protection of the Edisto River at the confluence of the Four Holes swamp. Composed largely of mature bottomland hardwood forest and mature mixed pine/hardwood upland and loblolly forest, this property will add protection to 2.8 miles of frontage along the Edisto River. In doing so, it will provide important storm water run-off mitigation to the nearby developable areas. The tract provides potential habitat to several wildlife species of concern, particularly spotted turtle and Swainson's Warbler. The dense thickets which occur along the property's edge, developed where sun light was able to penetrate from the cleared sand mining part of the tract, has created potentially great Swainson's habitat. Management in Beidler Forest focuses on expanding and improving habitat for migratory bird, which enhances habitat for a variety of other plant and animal communities.

property_description: The property leverages previous state, federal, and local conservation investments along the Catawba-Wateree River corridor by adding to the Landsford Canal Wildlife Management Area (WMA) which it abuts. Landsford Canal WMA subsequently abuts the historically significant Landsford Canal State Park at the river. Other conservation lands in the corridor include Katawba Valley Land Trust properties to the north and south as well as Catawba River WMA and Liberty Hill WMA to the south. Historic site management of the Landsford Addition tract consisted of silviculture in the uplands. The property will provide additional recreational hunting and fishing opportunities as well as a place for wildlife watching, hiking, and educational research (especially bats and herpetofauna). There is 12,000 years of human occupation on the property and likely colonial and antebellum occupation too. The Landsford Addition will benefit communities of plants and animals of conservation concern known or suspected on site. They include the Federally At-Risk plant species Georgia Aster and the Federally Endangered Carolina Heelsplitter, a freshwater mussel species known from waterways within the tract’s creek systems and river. Bottomlands and their associated uplands along river corridors are known for their importance to migratory bird species and are often a hotspot for biodiversity across a range of taxa. The tract and its surrounds should support at least 50 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) species of conservation concern and acreage under management, furthering efforts by the Southeast Conservation Adaption Strategy to reach a “10% or greater improvement in the health, function, and connectivity of Southeastern ecosystems by 2060.”
notes: Part of SCDNR's Landsford Canal Forest Legacy Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Langley Pond is 96 acres of good natural resources that currently adjoins an Aiken County Park that the County would like to expand. Aiken County contributed $100,000 in order to proceed with significant plans for developing this park into tourism and local area use, including: swimming, canoeing, gift shops, etc. Several streams transverse the property feeding Langley Pond and this tract has frontage on US #1.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Lawton Boggy tract is key acquisition to the Savannah River Preserve. The Savannah River Preserve program is an all-volunteer program started by concerned landowners who wish to see the areas along the Savannah River protected from encroaching development. This tract has 16 acres of bottomland along Boggy Branch, a Savannah River tributary. This area, which borders the Webb Center, is known for harboring tremendous biodiversity for birds.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Lawton Tract is part of the Savannah River Preserve Conservation Program. This "Program" was founded by concerned citizens of the Lowcountry who see development of similar lands and wish to maintain the beauty and wildness of their lands. These owners elect to sell conservation easements on their land for a flat rate of $250 an acre, well below market value. The Lawton Tract is adjacent to the Webb Wildlife Center and contains over 700 acres of forested wetlands. The acquisition of this easement will contribute to landscape connectivity and the linkage of critical wildlife habitat.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Legacy Farms Tract is a beautiful piece of undeveloped property located near the town of Luray in Hampton County. Located within the South Lowcountry (SoLo) focus area, this property is a classic example of a very well managed working timberland and recreational tract containing healthy stands of young longleaf pine plantation, mature loblolly pine quail woods, areas of variously aged planted loblolly pine, mixed upland hardwoods, bottomland hardwoods, and a large active agricultural field. The property contains frontage on both Black Creek and an unnamed tributary associated with Black Creek, both of which are part of the wetland system that make up the headwaters of the Coosawhatchie River, which flows into the Port Royal Sound, an extremely sensitive coastal embayment with unique ecological characteristics associated with highly productive estuarine habitat and recognized as one of the most pristine estuaries on the east coast.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Lemon Island Tract is 162.24 acres including marsh lands. It consists of a peninsula extended southeastward off of South Carolina Highway 170 and fronts the marshes of the Broad River on its southwest, east and northeast boundaries. This site has limited access to tidal water at a small hummuck in the southeastern point. Lemon Island includes five hummocks or marsh islands ranging from 0.092 to 2.4 acres. These islands are currently inaccessible from the mainland property but are located in high marsh and may have potential for causeway or light bridge access. Two of the islands have tidal creek access.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The most famous residents of this property are the fireflies Phausis reticulata. These fireflies appear in for two to four weeks in the late spring and emit a continuous light, rather then the blinking light of the common firefly. Locals refer to these flies as "ghost" or "fairy" flies because they emit a blue light.This fireflies have been documented in Annals of the Entomology Society of America. Aside from the most famous residents, the land is also home to black bear, turkey, deer, bobcat, songbirds, amphibians and reptiles. Mr. Dan Lewis, the owner of the property was married to the former South Carolina poet laureate, Bennie Lee Sinclair. The poet laureate referenced the fireflies in her most famous poem "The Dying. The Donor. The Phoenix." Mr. Lewis donated 50% of the value of the easement.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Liberty Hill Phase II Tract, with a total of 1,829.59 acres, is part of a purchase that created Liberty Hill WMA in Lancaster and Kershaw Counties. This tract has hardwood coves, mixed pine-hardwood slopes, loblolly pine ridgetops, and open meadows that provide habitat for game animals and an estimated 71 other terrestrial vertebrate and invertebrate priority species, as well as countless plants. Unique granitic boulders dot the landscape, giving the region the nickname, "the Devil's backbone." The tract as a whole is the last large block of unprotected lakefront (14 miles) in the region, 8 of which is included in this purchase. There are also unique scenic views including granitic rock outcrops along the shoreline, sandy beaches, high bluffs, and hidden coves.
notes: Part of SCDNR's Liberty Hill Wildlife Management Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This is phase 1 of the Liberty Hill proposal. The property has 14 total miles of waterfront on Lake Wateree and the land area resides in both Lancaster and Kershaw Counties. The property will eventually be turned over to SCDNR and has excellent potential to become a public park and WMA.
notes: Part of SCDNR's Liberty Hill Wildlife Management Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is comprised almost entirely of a Carolina Bay and borders 521 near Manning.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: LOCURA Tract is managed for forestry and wildlife near the US Sumter National Forest with a diversity of habitats and forest areas including loblolly pine stands and hardwood ravine areas. The hardwood area along the tributaries that feed into McClures Creek and the pond area are all very attractive to a variety of waterfowl species including wood ducks, egrets, herons and birds of prey. There is public viewing opportunities by virtue of having road frontage along Dave Jenkins Road which adds significantly to the scenic values enjoyed by the public enjoying recreational activities along the road. As this tract is located in the rolling hills of Fairfield County and according to Walter Edgar's book South Carolina History it was most likely a favorite hunting and camping spot for native peoples prior to European contact.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is located on SC Hwy 107 near Oconee State Park. This property adjoins a national forest and houses a historical cemetery on site. The tract has a good viewshed of the surrounding area, and the bottomlands of this property are prime soils located on East Village Creek.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Lyle Property preserves 165.89 acres of forest and open land in close proximity to Sumter National Forest. The property is composed of gently rolling foothills leading to the mountainous elevations of the national forest. Six flowing streams contribute over eight thousand feet of fresh water tributary and the southwestern border of the property is the center of Ramsey Creek encompassing nine hundred fifty feet.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is located 5 miles East of Sumter and is a typical small family working farm. There is an interior piece of this property totaling 59.6 acres which is already a WRP existing easement.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Marhaygue Farm Tract is managed for forestry and wildlife, within the "waterfowl corridor" of Lake Marion. A diversity of habitats and forest areas occur here that sustain healthy populations of all major game species in South Carolina. This land may also provide stop-over and resting habitats for the millions of migratory birds that pass through the Southeast in spring and fall migration. There is public access to approximately 375 acres of this property that allows access to trails connecting with the Santee Wildlife Refuge, research activities conducted within and around the Carolina Bay as well as a public landing road that traverses this property.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Mariwill Timber Plantation is managed for forestry and wildlife near the US Sumter National Forest with a diversity of habitats and forest areas including loblolly pine stands and hardwood ravine areas.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This magnificent tract of land contains over 8 miles of river frontage along the Great Pee Dee River. The area contains numerous Native American artifacts as well as habitat diversity for many animals including the bald eagle and the wood stork. The area also contains a forty acre lake which the public will have full access to. The entire area will be managed as a working forest and remain open to the public. If the property had not been purchased, a private developer would have subdivided the land and all public access would have been lost. This particular tract of land is located within the Upper Pee Dee and Lynches River Focus area, an international flagship project by the Atlantic Coast Joint Venture of the North American Waterfowl Management Plan. The owner of the land had every intention of selling before funds from the Conservation Bank were secured to ensure this property would not be lost.
notes: Part of SCDNR's Marsh Wildlife Management Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This project represents a unique opportunity to connect existing conservation easements, protecting 1,332 additional acres to create a contiguous privately-owned conservation area covering 5,500 acres across headwater streams of Cuffeytown Creek. This "Mays - Epworth Conservation Area" is named for the historic Epworth crossroads and Epworth Camp Meeting site, and to honor a landscape significant in the early life and learning of Dr. Benjamin Mays, a champion of non-violent protest, mentor to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr, theologian, writer, and university president. The Mays-Epworth Conservation Area (Adams) features a mosaic of open field, pine timberland, and hardwood bottoms and will bridge a 1-mile gap between existing easements near Epworth and along Cuffeytown Creek. Federally-protected lands (Sumter National Forest and Ninety Six National Historic Site) and several additional easements are close by. One of South Carolina's rarest trees, the Oglethorpe Oak, was documented here in the 1980s and may yet exist in the deeper woods of the project area, where Iredell Clay soils represent unique habitats. The properties are drained by headwater streams of Cuffeytown Creek, important for the Carolina Heelsplitter's downstream habitat and downstream water quality as well.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

recipient: Friends of Paris Mt State Park
property_description: The Arthur McCall Jr. Tract is an additional 160 acres of land that will be added to Paris Mountain State Park in Greenville County. This property includes 60 acres of forested lands with hardwoods along property lines and creek buffers and 100 acres of cleared or open lands where pine was recently cut. There are 2 small perennial creeks that flow into the lake and one small perennial creek flowing into the State Park. The purchase of this property represents a once-in-a-generation opportunity to preserve a large parcel adjacent to the Paris Mountain State Park that is geologically significant, biologically vital, and an important recreational resource for the 11 county Upstate Region. This property is also home to over 73 species of flora, over 20 species of vertebrates, and countless species of insects.
notes: Part of SCPRT's Paris Mountain State Park
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The McCorkle property adjoins a nature preserve operated by Spartanburg Area Conservancy. The addition of this piece of property protects an extra 1.5 miles of frontage on Lawson's Fork Creek. This creek is a major water source for residents of Spartanburg. If funds from the Conservation Bank had not been secured, this property would have been lost to development. This place is an outdoor enthusiasts dream. Runners utilize the 3 ½ miles of trails throughout the park while naturalists enjoy the 450 feet of boardwalk which extend over wetlands.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This impressive tract of land has over 3 miles of frontage on the Catawba River. This land will become part of the Heritage Preserve and will managed for total public use. This is an opportunity to preserve a rare expanse of undeveloped riverfront with development encroaching from both Columbia and Charlotte. The area is home to several bald eagle nests. There are also archeological and historical reasons for protecting this land. On nearby, Mount Dearborn Island, there rests the stone foundations of one of the nation's first arsenals built during the Revolutionary War.
notes: Part of SCDNR's Liberty Hill Wildlife Management Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

match_notes: Other: $62,050 KTHEP, $58,000 Oconee County Conservation Bank
property_description: The McKinney Creek Oconee Bell Preserve builds on Boones Creek Oconee Bell Preserve, located just north of Scenic Highway 11, next to Devil's Fork State Park, Sumter National Forest, Lake Jocassee and Lake Keowee. McKinney Creek is a critical habitat for the Oconee Bell, the signature species of the Jocassee and Keowee watersheds.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The McLeod Tract is an 375 acre tract located off Seabrook Road and U.S. Highway 21 with frontage at the Whale Branch River on Port Royal Island, Beaufort County, South Carolina. This property consists of former farmland, timber tracts, and woods of varying density.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Merchant Bank Building is an historic building located in Eastover. The building is on the historic register and has been a doctor's office, a library, a hardware store and the Merchant's Bank. The Conservation Bank’s funds will enable the Bank to be restored to its original condition and to be used as a welcome center.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

match_notes: Local: SCRCWF ($185,000) & Coastal Community Foundation ($600,000) OSI Loan: $1,620,000
property_description: The 974 acre Meyer Lake tract is located in Jasper County and contains the southernmost unprotected Savannah River floodplain bottomland hardwood forest in South Carolina. The tract has approximately 3.5 miles of Savannah River frontage and directly abuts a significant complex of permanently conserved lands totaling 54,331 acres, including the 31,551 acre Savannah National Wildlife Refuge and a 22,780 acre unbroken corridor of multiple privately and publicly preserved lands extending from the privately protected ~5,031 acre Exley Tract to the publicly accessible South Carolina Department of Natural Resources' (SCDNR) Tillman Sand Ridge Heritage Preserve which is located just under 20 river miles upstream.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Located on Little Cowhead Creek, this tract is mostly forested with a small pond on site.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract of land is a part of a continuing effort to preserve land along the Ashley River Historic District outside of Charleston. The Ashley River Historic District is a 13-mile corridor bound by the Ashley River and Ashley River Road. Along this stretch of land are remnants of civil war battles, post civil war African American settlements and Native American habitation. This land is under intense pressure from development. The Conservation Bank's funds were essential to the preservation of this property.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is the second phase of the Middleton proposal. The tract lies within the Ashley River Historic District. The Bank already has significant investment in this area, and the completion of this grant finalized the acquisition of over 5,000 acres in Dorchester County.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Mike and Tina Comalander Tract is manages for wildlife, agriculture and forestry with a diversity of habitats, including planted pin stands, pine hardwood forest, cove hardwood forest, piedmont bottomland hardwood riverine forest, and food plots of cultivated or grass cropland fields. Healthy populations of all major game species in South Carolina, including white-tailed deer, wild turkey, waterfowl, and small game occur here. Also present are species of furbearers such as otter, beaver, bobcat, mink, skunk, raccoon, fox and black bear. The bottom lands along Storm Creek and other small intermittent streams that feed Storm Creek may be home to wood ducks and to a lesser extent wading birds such as herons and egrets. During the dry periods along those streams one may see or hear quail, turkey, whip-poor-will and chuck-wills-widow.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Mill Shoals Community Forest protects critical wildlife corridors, water resources, the viewshed of Nine Times Preserve and will provide a recreation asset through the Wildlife Management Area program.
notes: Reimbursed $493,350
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: In 1890, Miss Eloise Miller's grandfather, an emancipated slave, began acquiring land whicheventually became a 200 acre farm. Miss Miller, who will be 95 years old in December, lives in the same house on the farm that she was born in. She describer the livestock, pecan grove, fruit orchard, and extensive agricultural fields that produces most of the food that the family lived on year round.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Millgrove Plantation is a +/- 440-acre property in Georgetown County located within the Winyah Bay Focus Area. This property is directly adjacent to the Black River, one of South Carolina's ten designated scenic rivers. The property has approximately 1,600 feet of direct Black River frontage creating scenic views for the public and clean water for downstream users. Millgrove Plantation is bisected by three roads, Rose Hill, Dunbar, and Benton Williams Roads, containing 13,600 feet of forested frontage. The tract is adjacent to Rocky Point Community Forest that is a publicly accessible park owned by the Winyah Rivers Alliance. The property is also just upstream from Ducks Unlimited 348 acre Winea Plantation. The property contains a diversity of habitat including 84 acres of forested and 24 acres of emergent wetlands. The upland areas primarily consist of planted loblolly pine and fields managed for the benefit of wildlife. The protection of Millgrove Plantation will secure the property from development as the demands for rural retreats and riverfront getaway destinations expand. Its protection would further increase the number of protected lands along the scenic Black River, supporting efforts by the conservation community to maintain its iconic beauty and conservation value.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The MillRho Investments, LLC property is comprised of upland pine plantations, bottomland hardwoods, isolated wetlands, mixes hardwood forests, open meadows, and sand ridges. Although the property is managed impressively for wildlife by itself, when placed in the larger landscape of protected farms and forests, the wildlife habitat value in impressive. This property has been occupied for centuries by Native Americans and settlers. The two cemeteries on the property are in relatively good condition, with markers dating back to the 1800s. In addition, the Orangeburg Stagecoach road runs through the property, which used to be a significant thoroughfare in the region.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This property is located on US #178 near the Edisto River and Limestone Creek. It is a Kings Grant property and an operational family farm with an old mill site dating back to 1790.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Culler family tracts are managed for agriculture, silviculture and wildlife on the North Fork Edisto River near Highway 178. A diversity of habitats and forest areas occur here, including loblolly and longleaf pine stands, mixed pine-hardwoods, riverine hardwoods and a 50 acre pond all of which support healthy populations of a variety of animal species. This property has floodplain bottomland hardwoods and oxbow lakes. Millwood Farms LLP drains to Limestone Creek, which has an old mill site and dam forming the 50 acre pond. The spillway drains back into Limestone Creek which then flows into the North Fork Edisto River. The fields have been terraced and the property has a vegetative buffer along the creek, pond, and river.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

match_notes: Local: Oconee Co CB ($10,000) Federal: NRCS ($67,500)
property_description: The 56-acre tract is located 6.2 miles southwest of the city of Seneca, South Carolina, and 6.7 miles east of the city of Westminster South Carolina. All of Oconee County continues to see the effect of rural development. The location of this parcel between two growing municipalities gives concern about the ability to keep it from the pressures of development. This property fronts SC Hwy. 24 and is located between the SC Scenic Hwy 11 corridor and Interstate 85 corridor. This is a family farm acquired from the owners' parents. It has been kept open and houses a small cattle operation. The property has two flowing streams that comprises 1324 linear feet of flow on the property. It has approximately 50 acres of pasture and 8.6 acres of forest and two bordering sides of the property are wildlife plantings, creating habitat between adjacent lands.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Morris Ford Tract has historically been an important crossing over the Salkehatchie River. The property is of unique archaeological significance since its military history spans the eighty-five between two wars. The conservation of this tract preserves important green space along the Salkehatchie River. This heavily wooded property is an excellent habitat for significant populations of forest inhabiting mammals, reptiles, amphibians, and invertebrates.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Perhaps no property better illustrates South Carolina's desire to preserve historical places more than the Morris Island Lighthouse. The first lighthouse was erected in 1762 to be replaced by a taller version several years later. In 1862 South Carolinians destroyed the lighthouse to prevent soldiers from using it as a lookout. In 1876, the current lighthouse was illuminated to be decommissioned and replaced by the Sullivan's Island Lighthouse (pictured in the background) in 1962. After being perilously close to development, the Morris Island Lighthouse has begun its long road to preservation this past spring. Funds from the Conservation Bank were crucial to the success of saving Morris Island. Morris Island is in the only lighthouse in the country to have an elevator.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Morrow Creek Timbers is nestled in the idyllic countryside of Abbeville County, just east of the Generostee Creek. The property consists primarily of hardwoods and features a spectacular array of wildlife. The property is home to wildlife such as white-tailed deer, beaver, turkey, grey and red fox, bobcats, coyotes, hogs, black bear, and two unique coveys of quail. The 6-acre pond and 30 acres of forested wetlands provide habitat for Wood Ducks, Black Ducks, Merganser, Mallards, Teal, Woodcocks, and Canada Geese. One acre of public access is provided adjacent to Old Rocky River Presbyterian Cemetery, which dates back to the 1700's. Access will be available from 7am until 7pm every day of the year. Notification of landowner is required. Contact Upstate Forever for more information.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This parcel of land is 175 acres of naturally significant and diverse land located directly on Scenic Highway 11 at the base of the Blue Ridge Mountains. This was the location of Camp Spearhead for years until the camp moved and the land was in critical danger of development. This camp was special because it provided handicapped access to many paths and natural features. Located along the Saluda River, this area has excellent habitat for wildlife. Future uses for this land could include park facility center or nature center as the infrastructure is already in place. The area provides a perfect spot to watch annual raptor migrations as 8,000-10,000 hawks are counted each year during migration season.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This private tract is located in the Cowassee Basin in the Whitemarsh Swamp. The area is all uplands and is part of the Midlands Area Joint Consortium Project which aligns compatible uses with neighboring military bases.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This is a large tract that fronts Colonel's creek and is located in Richland County and the Cowassee Basin. This tract adjoins other protected lands and is an addition to the previous two Murray tract phases.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_name: Myrtle Grove Plt - Marvin Tracts BC
property_description: The protection of Myrtle Grove Plantation - Marvin Tracts B&C is extremely important in that it completes the protection of all 2,073.21 acres of the landowner's property in the ACE Basin. It is also important to wildlife because it serves as a keystone piece in creating a connective corridor of protected lands spanning from the Combahee River to north of White Hall Road and the rail line. Protection of this tract will benefit numerous wildlife species. The land use on this property consists of 357.83 acres of wetland impoundments or historic rice fields. At present, the historic rice fields are minimally managed for waterfowl. The general public will benefit from the protection of Myrtle Grove Plantation since it is within close proximity to ACE Basin National Wildlife Refuge and is also visible along the 0.25 mile frontage on White Hall Road.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Myrtle Grove Plantation is located on SC State Highway 119 and the Combahee River in the ACE Basin. The property is situated on and accessed from White Hall Road having scenic road frontage, and is situated on and prominently visible by the public from the Combahee River. The property is in a relatively natural state containing approximately 1,767 acres of undeveloped land with a main residence, conservatory, equestrian barn, garages with 2nd floor apartments and other related improvements.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is located near the Tokeena Crossroads Project in Oconee County. This is a family farm including row crops, chicken houses and cattle. This tract sits between two developed areas.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This is the first tract the SC Conservation Bank has funded in Bamberg County. It contains portions of three separate Carolina Bays totaling 15 acres.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is located in the area between scenic HWY #11 and SC #178. The area is extremely diverse containing multiple rare and threatened flora and fauna species.  The  tract is currently under DNR management and is open to the public for hunting and fishing. The property has 9,900 feet of frontage on Nine Times Creek.
notes: Leased as a SCDNR Wildlife Management Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is located near scenic highway 11 in Pickens County. It is a very diverse tract that is home to various threatened species of flora and fauna. A property such as this with dense forests and beautiful views is in constant threat of development. It has 9,900 feet of frontage on Nine Times Creek, and adjoins to the previously approved Nine Times Tract A. This is an outstanding property for hunting and fishing, and it is currently under DNR management.
notes: Leased as a SCDNR Wildlife Management Area
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The North Enoree Wetland Tract contains 34 acres of bottomland hardwood forest and Piedmont Seep habitat intersperses with braided streams that flow into the North Enoree River. The property is almost entirely a wetland that is fueled by tributaries of the North Enoree and the Piedmont seeps that drain into the River. It is located directly off Tigerville Road, a major thoroughfare in Travelers Rest. With general public access, this property will facilitate easy access for universities, hikers and other forms of passive recreation. This tract's boundaries fall within close proximity to four established preserves.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Nowacki Tract is located in the 2500-acre Eastatoe Valley, a unique cove framed by the surrounding mountains of Jocassee Gorges. This tract is partially located on Wadakoe Mountain, one of the most botanically diverse mountains in the Southern Blue Ridge. There are significant habitat linkages for many game species, such as black bear, white tailed dear and turkey. The area is bounded on the north by the Eastatoe Creek, a drainage in the Savannah River Basin.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This magnificent piece of property is located on Wadmalaw Island outside of Charleston. This deep-water property is in a highly desirable location for development. The Charleston Greenbelt Commission paid half of the requested easement compensation.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Oakland Club Property presents a unique opportunity for the conservation community to protect an ecologically and culturally significant tract in the Santee River Focus Area. This property has frontage on approximately 10 miles of the high bluff of the Santee River Swamp, and contains thousands of acres of pine savannah, mature bottomland hardwood forest, and unique wetlands. Due to the landowners managing the property as an upland game hunting preserve and implementing a regular burn program on the pine savannah, they have developed some of the best habitat in the region for Bobwhite Quail and other upland game species. From a cultural standpoint, the property surrounds the burial ground of the Revolutionary War hero General Francis Marion's gravesite, which is open to the general public.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

match_notes: Local: Dorchester Trust Foundation Federal: NCWCGP
property_description: The Oaks Plantation permanently protects approximately 204 acres of maritime forest, mixed pine-hardwood forest, freshwater forested wetlands, and brackish marsh. This property provides important ecosystem services such as reducing storm surge impacts to downstream uplands; minimizing erosion and subsidence; supporting essential habitat for fisheries as well as threatened, endangered, and protected species; and providing research and recreational opportunities. The project considerably adds to the preservation and ecological integrity of the Ashley Scenic River, Ashley River Road Scenic Highway, and Ashley River Historic District (ARHD).
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Oconee Town Village site will protect one of the most significant archaeological, historical, and cultural assets of South Carolina's upstate. The property will connect with Sumter National Forest via the 210-acre Oconee Station, thus enlarging the protected landscape and providing an important extension for wildlife habitat. This area is known for its black bear, fox, bobcat, turkey, and pheasant. This property contains view of the stunning Tamassee Knob within Sumter National Forest. The land will be donated to SCPRT for inclusion in Oconee Station Historic Site which will allow visitors the chance to access Oconee Town through a network of trails once established by the Park.
notes: Part of SCPRT's Oconee Station State Historic Site
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Old Santee Canal (OSC) property is situated on the Santee River with 1.9 miles of scenic river frontage. Its high bluffs overlook the Santee and provide stunning views both from the river and land side. In terms of historical sites, locks 1 and 2 of the Old Santee Canal as well as the canal itself are located on the property. Lock 1 is located adjacent to the Santee River, and lock 2 is in the interior of the property. Thomas Walter's gravesite is also located within the property. The OSC property is mostly forested with a mixture of native hardwood species as well as pine stands in various age classes. Approximately 211 acres of the property are classified as forested wetlands according to National Wetlands Inventory data. The property is accessible from SC Highway 45 and is situated within a corridor of protected properties along the Santee River
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: This tract is located within the ACE Basin between SC #174 and the Intracoastal Waterway. It adjoins several other tracts previously funded by the bank and is in a high-development area.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Paris Mountain Expansion Tract will add another 33 acres the Paris Mountain State Park to prevent further fragmentation of the park and allow the forest-dwelling wildlife to continue ranging beneath a mature hardwood canopy. The property contains the headwaters to a mountain creek that feeds into the larger Buckhorn Creek. On the northern edge of this tract is an intact ridgeline that shares its border with another property and enjoys expansive views during the winter. For the State Park's 250,000 annual visitors, this property is an asset and one that could potentially result in a mile-long loop trail to connect into the park. This is an ideal property to help further protect the park from development and secure its ecological integrity for the wildlife that roams its forests.
notes: Part of SCPRT's McGee Paris Mountain Extension
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: The Paris Mountain Gospel Tract overlooks Furman University and the Swamp Rabbit Trail. The plan for this property is to create a trail system that will connect to the back half of Paris Mountain State Park and the Swamp Rabbit Trail.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: Patriots Plantation II contains 1,867.5 acres including 515 acres of forested lands, 39.5 acres of cleared/open lands, and 1,313 acres of wetlands. This property also has 1.2 miles of frontage on the Great Pee Dee River and 3.4 miles of frontage on Clarks Creek. Patriots Plantation was selected to protect freshwater wetland habitat on the South Carolina Coastal Plain. This property's wetland habitat plays an important role for many species of migratory waterfowl by providing some of the most extensive, intact wetlands in the southeastern United States.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

property_description: St. Helena Island is one the few remaining regions in Beaufort County that still retains it agricultural heritage and a prominent Gullah culture. The Sanders family has been farming for years as the soil here is among the finest in the state. The family farm is located near the PennCenter which is historically significant as the first school to be opened for newly freed slaves along the South Carolina coast after the Civil War. The Conservation Bank contributed funds along with the USDA's Farm and Ranch Land Protection Program and Beaufort County's Rural and Critical Lands Program to ensure the continuation of this farming community. Without assistance, this prime farmland would have been turned into prime real estate land.
source: SC Conservation Bank grants feature service

The property is a hotspot for biodiversity, with more than 68 Species of Greatest Conservation Need in the immediate area as identified in South Carolina’s State Wildlife Action Plan. Of these, 35 are identified by SEAFWA as Regional Species of Greatest Conservation Need. Protection of the property will conserve the function and value of approximately 206 acres of total wetlands and 105 acres of managed wildlife impoundments. The property will provide meaningful public recreational opportunities for hikers, hunters, bird watchers, and wildlife enthusiasts as well as be open for university research.

property_description: This 446-acre historic site is the centerpiece of the SCDNR Scenic Broad River Plan and forms the foundation of NFLT’s Broad River focus area. The Broad River presents an undeveloped riverfront of Piedmont forests and pasturelands. The riparian forest is home to diverse native plant and animal life. Eagles, ospreys, and other birds frequent the river corridor. The high River bluffs have natural beech trees with a natural understory, supporting plant species not normally found this far north. The creation of the Broad Scenic River Plan with SCDNR focused on Smith Ford Farm as an example of the significance of the 15-mile segment of the Broad River between Cherokee and York counties. Smith Ford and the area surrounding the river are rich with historical features: from the original Smith's Ford to Native American fishing weir traps in the River. The Farmhouse was constructed in 1790, is included in the YC Survey of Historic Architecture in 1992, and is National Register Eligible. Smith Ford is actually a crossroad of American history as it was used by troops during the American Revolutionary and Civil Wars. The site has 1.6 miles of riverfront along the Broad River, particularly the Smith Ford which was used by the Cherokee and Catawba Indians, and by retreating Confederate troopers detailed to Jefferson Davis during his flight after the fall of Richmond. It served as the District Post Office and a ferry operated of the property.

This sea island is in the heart of the National Park Service's Gullah-Geechee Cultural Heritage Corridor and was once owned by a former slave. property_description: The Spring Park and Spring Park Inn project seeks to create a destination park in the renovated city center directly adjacent to the Swamp Rabbit Trail, which hosts thousands of bikers, walkers, and hikers every week. The 20-acre tract formerly known as Spring Park on Main Street in the heart of downtown Travelers Rest is still undeveloped open space, currently leased to a golf driving range. Adjoining the Park is a two-story house constructed circa 1820, which is the residence of Nell Gibson, an 88-year-old lifetime resident of Travelers Rest. Originally built as a private residence, the house transitioned to use as an inn by 1852 and continued housing travelers until 1941 as The Spring Park Inn. For almost 100 years, travelers on their way to and from North Carolina stayed at the Inn. In 1889 Robert Anderson, owner of the Inn, conveyed one and a half acres in front of the Inn for construction of a railroad platform and the Inn became a stopping place on the Swamp Rabbit Railroad, which is now the Swamp Rabbit Trail. The Spring Park Inn is on both the federal and South Carolina Registers of Historic Places.

property_description: The Stateline Blue Ridge Tract is a short drive from the rapidly expanding downtown of Landrum.
